title: DOG Practice Test - Reading Comprehension
description: A 40-question reading practice test modeled after the attached packet format: 5 passages, 8 multiple-choice questions per passage. The information is different from the original document.
directions: Read each passage carefully. Then answer the questions by choosing A, B, C, or D.

passages.title: The Radio in the Window
passages.text:
In 1944, Nora lived with her parents in a small town in North Carolina. Her father worked at the train station, and her older cousin David had gone away to serve during World War II. Every evening after supper, Nora helped Mama wash dishes, then hurried to the front room where the family radio sat beside the window.

Most nights, the radio played music or news reports. Nora listened carefully, hoping to hear something that might tell her David was safe. Mama always told her, “News travels slowly, but hope can travel fast.” Nora did not fully understand what Mama meant, but she liked the sound of it.

One rainy Thursday, the announcer read a short message from soldiers overseas. Nora heard David’s unit mentioned. Her heart beat quickly. The message did not name David, but it said that the unit was safe after a difficult journey. Mama reached for Nora’s hand, and they both smiled with tears in their eyes.

The next morning, Nora wrote David a letter. She told him about the rain, the garden, and the way Mama’s biscuits filled the kitchen with warmth. At the end she wrote, “We heard good news, and we are keeping hope by the window.” When she placed the letter in the mailbox, Nora felt a little braver than before.

passages.title: The Busy Life of Sea Turtles
passages.text:
Sea turtles are reptiles that live mostly in the ocean. They have strong flippers that help them swim long distances. Unlike land turtles, sea turtles cannot pull their heads and flippers inside their shells. Their bodies are built for moving through water.

Female sea turtles return to sandy beaches to lay eggs. At night, a mother turtle crawls out of the ocean, digs a nest in the sand, and lays many eggs. Then she covers the nest and returns to the sea. Weeks later, baby turtles hatch and crawl toward the ocean. They use moonlight and the bright horizon over the water to guide them.

Sea turtles help keep ocean habitats healthy. Some eat seagrass, which helps the grass grow strong. Others eat jellyfish, sponges, or small sea animals. Each kind of sea turtle has a role in the ocean ecosystem.

Today, sea turtles face dangers from pollution, fishing nets, and bright lights near beaches. Plastic bags can look like jellyfish in the water, and turtles may try to eat them. People can help by cleaning beaches, reducing plastic waste, and keeping nesting beaches dark at night.

passages.title: The Dog and the Little Sparrow
passages.text:
One spring morning, a young dog named Milo chased butterflies across a field. He barked happily and ran so fast that he did not notice a tiny sparrow sitting near a fallen branch.

“Please be careful,” chirped the sparrow. “My wing is hurt, and I cannot fly away.”

Milo stopped at once. He was excited to keep playing, but he knew the little bird needed help. Gently, he nudged the branch aside and sat nearby to keep other animals away. When the farmer’s daughter walked past, Milo barked softly until she noticed the sparrow. She picked up the bird and placed it safely in a small basket.

A few weeks later, Milo wandered too far from the farmhouse. The sky grew dark, and he could not find the path home. Suddenly, a sparrow flew above him, chirping again and again. Milo followed the sound through the tall grass until he saw the warm lights of the farmhouse.

The sparrow landed on the fence and sang a bright song. Milo wagged his tail. He understood that kindness, once given, often finds its way back.
passages.moral: Kindness given to others may return when you need it most.

passages.title: The First School Bus
passages.text:
Long ago, many children walked several miles to school each day. Some rode horses or wagons, but many students had no easy way to travel. During cold mornings or rainy weather, getting to school could be difficult.

In the late 1800s, some communities began using wagons to carry children to school. These early school vehicles were sometimes called school wagons. Horses pulled them along dirt roads. The ride was slow and bumpy, but it helped more children arrive safely.

As automobiles became more common, motorized school buses replaced horse-drawn wagons. Over time, school buses became stronger, safer, and easier to recognize. Many buses were painted yellow because the bright color helped drivers see them clearly.

Today, school buses carry millions of students. They have stop signs, flashing lights, and safety rules to protect children. The school bus changed how students traveled and made it easier for many children to attend school regularly.

passages.title: A Rainy Afternoon
passages.text:
Rain taps softly on the glass,
Silver drops slide down,
Clouds wear coats of quiet gray
Above the sleepy town.

Puddles shimmer near the road,
Boots splash through the street,
A robin shakes its little wings
And sings a song so sweet.

Inside, the kettle hums with warmth,
A book waits by the chair,
The world feels calm and washed and new,
With music in the air.

Rainy days may dim the sky,
Yet gentle wonders grow;
A quiet heart can hear the song
That raindrops softly know.
